text: Foundations defined what a data policy is. Chapter two of this course is about what produces one for real — the document template and the process behind it.

A real policy document has seven sections: a title and policy ID, purpose and rationale, scope borrowed from the charter, the policy statement itself, a named owner and approver from the RACI matrix, an effective date and review cycle, and links to the standards that implement it.

Draft — the steward writes it, owner gives context. Review — legal, compliance, and IT weigh in. Approve — the governance committee signs off, sponsor backs anything organization-wide. Publish — somewhere central and discoverable. Review on a set cadence, not just once.

Naming a specific tool inside the policy ages it badly — that's a standard's job. No named owner means no one updates or defends it. No stated scope makes it unenforceable. And no review cadence means it quietly goes stale while the business changes underneath it.
Next lesson: the companion document a policy is only half the story without — standards and procedures.
